CSCI3180 Principles of Programming Languages

Introduction

Consider a program in language $\mathcal{L}$. We care about mainly two things: (1) Syntax (definition of set $\mathcal{L}$) and Semantic (how the program in $\mathcal{L}$ does). Mathematically, we can treat interpreter as a partial function that maps from the language to values: $$\text{Interpreter}_{\mathcal{L}} : \mathcal{L} \rightharpoonup \mathcal{V}$$

Whereas compiler is a function between two languages where $$ \text{Interpreter}_{\mathcal{L}_1} = \text{Interpreter}_{\mathcal{L}_2} \circ \text{Compiler}_{\mathcal{L}_1 \rightarrow \mathcal{L}_2}$$

Sometimes we create syntactic sugar, for instance (not e) === (if e then true else false). We can denote this relation as $$ \text{Evaluator}_{\mathcal{L}} = \text{Evaluator}_{\mathcal{L}_\text{core}} \circ \text{Desugarer}_{\mathcal{L}} $$

Target: Can we create an abstracted mathematical model for programs?

Syntax and Formal Language

Backus-Naur Form (BNF) is a way for us to specify the grammar of a language. An example for boolean is t ::= true | false | t and t | t or t, where t is called metavariables (to distinguish with actual variables). Given such a grammar, we can create the parse tree of any syntactically valid term, forming the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) and can be translated to Algebraic Data Type (ADT) in programming languages.

We can define potentials on ASTs such as constants, size and depth, and carry out Structural Induction on AST (since, well, they are rooted trees). Well-founded relation are partial order $\prec$ such that there does not exists infinite descending chain, which we can induct on it.

Simply refer to CSCI3130 Notes for more details.

Semantics

There are three styles of discussing semantics, as listed as follows:

  1. Operational Semantics: state |- term -> (new term, new state)
  2. Denotational Semantics: [[term]] := state -> value
  3. Axiomatic Semantics: (Hoare triple) {predicate P} program {predicate Q}

Each of them are slightly different, but yet the main idea is the same: to find out the axiomatic inference rules for basic programming blocks (boolean, if-then-else, while-loop, etc), and use them to apply on everything.

Rewriting System over language $\mathcal{L}$ is a relation $\rightarrow$ over $\mathcal{L} \times \mathcal{L}$ where we can replace $x \in \mathcal{L}$ by $y$ iff $x \rightarrow y$, which is called (small-step) reduction. We denote its transitive closure, (big-step) evaluation, as $x \Downarrow y$ (equivalently $x \rightarrow^* y$). A proof system is a special case where we derive with truth value ($\top$) and false value ($\bot$).

A rewriting system $(\mathcal{L}, \rightarrow)$ is confluent iff for all $w \in \mathcal{L}$ we have $w \Downarrow x \land w \Downarrow y \implies x \Downarrow z \land y \Downarrow z$ for some $z \in \mathcal{L}$, which is exactly when the evaluated result is deterministic (note the actual evaluation is not required to be deterministic for this). Meanwhile, we call $\rightarrow$ terminating if for all $x \in \mathcal{L}$, any reduction chain is finite, which is exactly when $\rightarrow$ is well-founded.

We call $x \in \mathcal{L}$ to be in normal form iff $x$ cannot be further reduced, while a subset of normal form is considered as values which is the set of expected results. Non-value normal form normally indicates the program has gotten stuck.

Untyped Imperative Language

There are two main components: The syntactic form (syntax) and evaluation rules (semantics). First, arithmetics:

Booleans $\mathbb{B}$

Syntactic Forms
  • Terms t ::= true | false | if t then t else t
  • Values v ::= true | false
Evaluation Rules
  • if true then t2 else t3 -> t2
  • if false then t2 else t3 -> t3
  • t1 -> t1' => if t1 then t2 else t3 -> if t1' then t2 else t3

Natural Numbers $\mathbb{N}$

Syntactic Forms
  • Terms t ::= 0 | succ t | pred t | iszero t
  • Values v ::= nv
  • Numeric Values nv ::= 0 | succ nv

The evaluation rules are just common senses so I omit them. The above are in the style of small-step operational semantics.

Simple Imperative Language (SIMPL)

Syntactic Forms
  • Terms t ::= v | skip | r := t (assignment) | !r (deference) | t1; t2 (sequence) | if t1 then t2 else t3 | while t1 do t2 | t1 op t2
  • Operators op ::= + | - | * | / | <=
  • Values v ::= b: bool | z: int

Common sense prevails. One may deduce the evaluation rules in both small-step and big-step operation semantics.

Functions

Idea: can we encode functions as objects? Turns out we can!

Lambda Calculus (λ)

Syntactic Forms
  • Terms t ::= x | λx. t (abstraction) | t1 t2 (application)
  • Values v ::= x | λx. t
Evaluation Rules
  • t1 -> t1' => t1 t2 -> t1' t2
  • t2 -> t2' => t1 t2 -> t1 t2'
  • (λx. t) v -> [x |-> v] t or t[v/x]

The binder λx has its scope extends rightwards. A variable $x$ is bounded if it is in scope of some λx, and free otherwise. A λ-term without free variables is called closed and is a combinator. It is possible to have nameless version of λ-Calculus by replacing variable names with integers. Capture-avoiding Substitution is always done, which simply means when substitution we avoid captures to not change the meaning.

A term of the form (λx. t) v is called a redex (reducible expression). There are different evaluation strategies: (1) beta-reduction: reduce everything (Church-Rosser Theorem states that this is confluent); (2) call-by-name: only reduce term outside abstraction, and from out to in; (3) call-by-value: only reduce term outside abstraction, and from in to out; (4) call-by-need: only lazily call when needed by using thunks, which abstracts the function to a value in a call-by-value scenario, whereas memorisation can also be done. Infinite lazy list can be defined as well.

The Church Encoding allows us to express everything in λ-Calculus:

Church Boolean
  • tru = λt. λf. t (true)
  • fls = λt. λf. f (false)
  • test = λl. λm. λn. l m n (if-then-else)
Church Pair
  • pair = λf. λs. λb. b f s
  • fst = λp. p tru
  • snd = λp. p fls
Church Numeral
  • c0 = λs. λz. z
  • cn = λs. λz. sn(z)
  • scc = λn. λs. λz. s (n s z)

Simple Abstract Machine Language (SAML)

Syntactic Forms
  • Terms t ::= id | if t1 then t2 else t3 | fun args -> t | t1 t2 | let bind in t | op t | t1 binop t2 | let rec x = fun x -> t in t
  • Bindings bind ::= x = e | x = e, bind
  • Identifiers id ::= x | z | b
  • Arguments args ::= x | x args
  • Binary Operators binop ::= + | - | * | / | and | or | <=
  • Unitary Operator op ::= not
  • Values v ::= z | b | fun args -> t

For a matter of fact, some of the above -> are actually partial functions, but one may just interpret them using common sense.

Recursion

How to define recursions in λ-Calculus? In fact, for f: X -> Y we can define F : (X -> Y) -> X -> Y that maps f to f'. By fix f = λf. (λx. f(λy. x x y)) (λx. f(λy. x x y)), we have fix F = F(fix F) a fixed point of F, which is computes the result of the recursion given that it terminates.

Scoping

There are two major types of scoping: (1) Lexical (Static) scoping, which the scope is deduced from syntax; (2) Dynamic Scoping, which the scope is deduced from semantics, e.g., OCaml is static scoping. In many languages, there are also global scope and local scope, and we can alias variables.

With (mutable) environment (in constract with immutable context), we can no longer treat functions as first-class, and we need to treat function along the environment as a closure.

Typed System

Types are used to detect errors in programs statically before even running the programs. The typing relation t: T can be introduced with inductive typing rules.

Typing system can be as well treated as a proof system of propositions in the form "The term t is of type T". The typing relation is the (smallest) relation between terms and types satisfying the typing rules.

Well-typed and Type Safety

A term t is well-typed if its type can be deduced from the syntax alone, without resort to semantics. For example, "if true then 0 else false" evaluates to 0 and has the type of Nat (|= if true then 0 else false: Nat), but it is not well-typed and we cannot prove the type according to the typing rules.

A type system is safe when combining (1) progress (well-typed term does not stuck) and (2) preservation (well-typed term stays well-typed after reduction).

Denote Γ be the typing context, a map between variables and their types. Then for λ-Calculus we have

  • (Abstraction) Γ, x: T1 |- t2: T2 => Γ |- λx: T1. t2 : T1 -> T2
  • (Application) Γ |- t1: T1 -> T2, Γ |- t2: T1 => Γ |- t1 t2 : T2

Well-typed terms under simple systems are always normalisable (halts and reduces to value).

Side Notes

Curry-Howard Correspondence is the correspondence between propositions and types, which we can treat the typing of a term as the proposition it proves. Curry-style systems are implicit which allows non well-typed terms, meanwhile Church-style systems disallow ill-typed terms at all.

Extensions can be made to the typing system, for example unit, sequencing, ascriptions, let bindings, tuples, records, sums, lists and variants.

Polymorphism includes parametric polymorphism (type variables), ad-hoc polymorphism (overloading names) and subtype polymorphism (inherit classes).

Subtyping $<:$ is defined as as where $\tau \lt: \tau'$ iff $\tau$ is a subtype of $\tau'$, and it is safe to use $\tau'$ in place of $\tau$.

Recursive Types

Recursive types are of the form list = <nil: unit, cons: {T, list}>. We can introduce the recursion operator µ where the types are defined recursively. For example, list = µX. <nil: unit, cons: {T, X}>, whereas stream = µA. unit -> {T, A}. We can then introduce the typed fixed-point combinator as fixT = λf: T -> T. (λx: (µA. A -> T). f(x x)) (λx: (µA. A -> T). f(x x)).

There are two ways of treating recursive types, namely equi-recursive (folds is equivalent) or iso-recursive (folds is isomorphic only).

Formally we consider operator (generating functions) on power set on $\mathcal{U} \times \mathcal{U}$, the set of all typing relations. Denote $F$ be monotone if $X \subset Y \implies F(X) \subset Y$. Then $X$ is F-closed iff $F(X) \subset X$ and is F-consistent if $X \subset F(X)$, and fixed point if $F(X) = X$. Knaster-Tarski theorem states that intersection of all F-closed sets is the least fixed point µF, whereas the union of all F-consistent sets is the greatest fixed point νF.
